# Unit 1: Kinematics

## Overview
**Kinematics** describes motion using position, **displacement**, **velocity**, **acceleration**, time, and graphs—without yet explaining the forces that cause the motion. This unit matters heavily on the AP Physics 1 exam because students must interpret motion representations, connect equations to graphs, and analyze situations like **constant-acceleration motion** and **projectile motion**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Position** | An object’s location relative to a chosen origin. | AP questions often require careful use of a **coordinate system** and sign conventions. |
| **Displacement** | Change in position: how far and in what direction an object moves from start to finish. | Students must distinguish **displacement** from **distance traveled**, especially in graph and verbal questions. |
| **Velocity** | Rate of change of position; includes direction. | AP problems test both **average velocity** and **instantaneous velocity**, often from graphs. |
| **Acceleration** | Rate of change of velocity. | A central AP idea: nonzero acceleration does **not** always mean speeding up. |
| **Constant-Acceleration Motion** | Motion in which acceleration remains constant over time. | Students must apply **kinematic equations** and connect them to graph shapes. |
| **Motion Graphs** | **Position-time**, **velocity-time**, and **acceleration-time** graphs. | AP questions frequently ask for slope, area, and qualitative graph interpretation. |
| **Projectile Motion** | Two-dimensional motion with independent horizontal and vertical components. | A classic AP topic requiring decomposition into axes and use of constant vertical acceleration. |
| **Reference Frames and Sign** | The choice of positive direction and origin. | Many AP mistakes come from inconsistent signs for position, velocity, and acceleration. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose coordinate system and define positive direction] --> B[Identify known quantities]
    B --> C[Determine if acceleration is constant]
    C --> D{One-dimensional or two-dimensional motion?}
    D -->|One-dimensional| E[Use graphs and kinematic equations]
    D -->|Two-dimensional| F[Separate motion into x and y components]
    F --> G[Horizontal: usually constant velocity]
    F --> H[Vertical: constant acceleration]
    G --> I[Combine component results]
    H --> I
    E --> J[Check signs, units, and physical meaning]
    I --> J
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Quantity / Rule** | **Expression** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Displacement** | $$\Delta x = x_f - x_i$$ | Change in position. |
| **Average velocity** | $$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$$ | Slope of a secant line on a position-time graph. |
| **Average acceleration** | $$a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ | Change in velocity per unit time. |
| **Velocity under constant acceleration** | $$v = v_0 + at$$ | Final velocity after time $$t$$. |
| **Position under constant acceleration** | $$x = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$ | Position as a function of time. |
| **Velocity-position relation** | $$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)$$ | Useful when time is not given. |
| **Average velocity for constant acceleration** | $$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}$$ | Only valid for constant acceleration. |
| **Horizontal projectile motion** | $$x = x_0 + v_{0x}t$$ | Horizontal acceleration is often $$0$$. |
| **Vertical projectile motion** | $$y = y_0 + v_{0y}t + \frac{1}{2}a_y t^2$$ | Usually $$a_y = -g$$ if up is positive. |
| **Velocity components** | $$v_{0x} = v_0 \cos\theta,\qquad v_{0y} = v_0 \sin\theta$$ | Break launch velocity into components. |
| **Near-Earth gravitational acceleration** | $$g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$$ | On many AP problems, use consistent sign convention. |

### Graph Relationships You Must Know
- **Slope of position-time graph** $$\rightarrow$$ **velocity**
- **Slope of velocity-time graph** $$\rightarrow$$ **acceleration**
- **Area under velocity-time graph** $$\rightarrow$$ **displacement**
- **Area under acceleration-time graph** $$\rightarrow$$ **change in velocity**

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Related Concepts** | **Connection / Difference** | **AP Importance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Distance vs. Displacement** | **Distance** is total path length; **displacement** is net change in position. | AP free-response and MCQs often punish confusing scalar and vector quantities. |
| **Speed vs. Velocity** | **Speed** is scalar; **velocity** includes direction. | A negative velocity is meaningful; a negative speed is not. |
| **Velocity vs. Acceleration** | Velocity describes motion; acceleration describes how velocity changes. | An object can have positive velocity and negative acceleration at the same time. |
| **Horizontal vs. Vertical Projectile Motion** | Horizontal and vertical motions are analyzed independently, but share the same time. | This independence is essential for solving projectile questions correctly. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Position] --> B[Displacement]
    B --> C[Velocity]
    C --> D[Acceleration]
    E[Velocity-time graph] --> F[Area gives displacement]
    G[Position-time graph] --> H[Slope gives velocity]
    I[Acceleration-time graph] --> J[Area gives change in velocity]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **distance traveled** with **displacement**. If an object turns around, the two are not the same.
- Assuming that if **acceleration** is negative, the object must be slowing down. It slows down only when **velocity** and **acceleration** have opposite signs.
- Using kinematic equations when **acceleration is not constant**. Those equations are valid only for constant acceleration.
- Forgetting that in **projectile motion**, horizontal acceleration is usually $$0$$ while vertical acceleration is $$-g$$ or $$+g$$ depending on the chosen axis.
- Reading graphs incorrectly: on a **position-time** graph, height is position, but **slope** is velocity.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can distinguish **position**, **displacement**, **distance**, **speed**, and **velocity**.
- [ ] I can calculate **average velocity** and **average acceleration** from words, data, or graphs.
- [ ] I can choose and apply the correct **kinematic equation** for constant-acceleration motion.
- [ ] I can interpret the **slope** and **area** relationships for motion graphs.
- [ ] I can explain how an object may be moving in the positive direction while accelerating in the negative direction.
- [ ] I can analyze **projectile motion** by separating it into horizontal and vertical components.
- [ ] I can use a consistent **sign convention** and justify my answers physically.
- [ ] I can determine whether an answer makes sense based on units, direction, and the motion described.

# Unit 2: Force and Translational Dynamics

## Overview
This unit introduces **Newton’s three laws of motion** and the idea that **forces** change an object’s motion by causing **acceleration**. You’ll learn how to identify and analyze forces such as **gravity**, **normal force**, **tension**, and **friction**, especially through **free-body diagrams** and equilibrium reasoning.

This unit matters on the AP exam because many problems begin with correct **force identification** and then require you to connect those forces to motion using **Newton’s Second Law**. Strong skill with force diagrams and vector reasoning is essential for both multiple-choice and free-response questions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Force** | An interaction that can change an object’s velocity; a vector quantity. | AP questions often test whether you can identify all forces acting on a system and reason about their directions. |
| **Newton’s First Law** | An object remains at rest or in constant-velocity motion unless acted on by a net external force. | Helps distinguish **equilibrium** from **acceleration** and explains why balanced forces mean no change in motion. |
| **Newton’s Second Law** | The net force on an object is related to its mass and acceleration. | This is the central quantitative tool of the unit and appears constantly in problem solving. |
| **Newton’s Third Law** | Forces between interacting objects come in equal-magnitude, opposite-direction pairs acting on different objects. | A common AP trap is confusing third-law pairs with forces that cancel on the same object. |
| **Free-Body Diagram** | A simplified diagram showing all external forces acting on one object. | Correct free-body diagrams are often the key first step in solving force problems correctly. |
| **Normal Force** | A contact force exerted by a surface, perpendicular to that surface. | Students often assume it always equals weight; AP questions frequently test when that is false. |
| **Friction** | A contact force parallel to the surface that opposes relative motion or attempted motion. | AP problems often require distinguishing **static** from **kinetic** friction and using the correct inequality or equation. |
| **Translational Equilibrium** | A state in which the net force is zero, so acceleration is zero. | Important for analyzing objects at rest or moving at constant velocity and for setting up force component equations. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify the object or system] --> B[Draw a free-body diagram]
    B --> C[Choose coordinate axes]
    C --> D[Resolve angled forces into components]
    D --> E[Write net force equations in each direction]
    E --> F["Apply Newton's Second Law: $$\sum F_x = ma_x$$ and $$\sum F_y = ma_y$$"]
    F --> G{Is acceleration zero?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Use equilibrium conditions]
    G -->|No| I[Solve for acceleration or unknown force]
    H --> J[Interpret motion: rest or constant velocity]
    I --> J
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Rule** | **Expression or Statement** | **Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Newton’s First Law** | If $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$, then velocity is constant. | Determines when an object is in **translational equilibrium**. |
| **Newton’s Second Law** | $$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$ | Core equation relating forces to acceleration. |
| **Component form of Newton’s Second Law** | $$\sum F_x = ma_x$$ and $$\sum F_y = ma_y$$ | Used when forces act in different directions. |
| **Newton’s Third Law** | If object A exerts a force on object B, then object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A. | Identifies interaction pairs correctly. |
| **Weight** | $$F_g = mg$$ | The gravitational force near Earth’s surface. |
| **Static friction** | $$f_s \leq \mu_s N$$ | Static friction adjusts up to a maximum value. |
| **Maximum static friction** | $$f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$ | Used when an object is just about to slip. |
| **Kinetic friction** | $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ | Used when surfaces are sliding relative to each other. |
| **Equilibrium condition** | $$\sum F_x = 0,\quad \sum F_y = 0$$ | Applies when acceleration is zero. |
| **Inclined plane force components** | Parallel to incline: $$mg\sin\theta$$; perpendicular to incline: $$mg\cos\theta$$ | Very common setup on AP problems involving ramps. |

### Must-know force rules
- **Normal force** is perpendicular to a surface, not always equal to $$mg$$.
- **Tension** in an ideal rope is the same throughout the rope if the rope is massless and passes over frictionless pulleys.
- **Friction** always acts parallel to the contact surface and opposes relative motion or attempted motion.
- A **free-body diagram** should include only forces acting **on** the object, not forces the object exerts on something else.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Similarities** | **Key Difference** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Static vs. Kinetic Friction** | Both are contact forces parallel to the surface and oppose relative motion. | **Static friction** varies up to a maximum; **kinetic friction** usually has constant magnitude $$\mu_k N$$ once sliding begins. | Students often incorrectly set $$f_s = \mu_s N$$ in every static case. |
| **Weight vs. Normal Force** | Both can act vertically in some problems and are often compared in equilibrium situations. | **Weight** is gravitational and equals $$mg$$; **normal force** is a contact force from a surface and depends on the situation. | AP often tests cases where $$N \ne mg$$, such as inclines or vertical acceleration. |
| **Balanced vs. Unbalanced Forces** | Both describe the total set of forces acting on an object. | **Balanced forces** give $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$; **unbalanced forces** give $$\sum \vec{F} \ne 0$$ and produce acceleration. | Important for connecting force diagrams to motion descriptions. |
| **Newton’s Third-Law Pair vs. Forces That Cancel** | Both involve equal and opposite forces. | Third-law pairs act on **different objects**; canceling forces act on the **same object**. | One of the most common conceptual MCQ traps. |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Assuming the **normal force** always equals $$mg$$. On an incline or in vertical acceleration, it often does not.
- Treating **static friction** as always equal to $$\mu_s N$$. Really, $$f_s$$ adjusts as needed up to its maximum.
- Confusing **Newton’s Third-Law pairs** with balanced forces. Third-law forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel in one free-body diagram.
- Drawing extra forces on a free-body diagram, such as “motion” or “inertia.” Only actual interactions produce forces.
- Forgetting to resolve forces into **components** when axes are tilted or when forces act at angles.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can state and apply **Newton’s First, Second, and Third Laws**.
- [ ] I can draw a correct **free-body diagram** for a single object.
- [ ] I can identify **weight**, **normal force**, **tension**, and **friction** in a physical situation.
- [ ] I can determine whether forces are **balanced** or **unbalanced** and relate that to acceleration.
- [ ] I can write and solve $$\sum F_x = ma_x$$ and $$\sum F_y = ma_y$$ for an object.
- [ ] I can distinguish **static friction** from **kinetic friction** and use the correct equation or inequality.
- [ ] I can analyze forces on an **inclined plane**, including $$mg\sin\theta$$ and $$mg\cos\theta$$ components.
- [ ] I can explain why **Newton’s Third-Law pairs** act on different objects and do not cancel in one diagram.

# Unit 3: Work, Energy, and Power

## Overview
This unit develops the **work-energy theorem**, the idea of **conservative forces**, and the use of **energy conservation** to analyze motion without tracking every force over time. It matters on the AP exam because many problems become much simpler when you shift from **Newton’s laws** to **energy methods**, especially for ramps, springs, gravity, and power situations.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Work** | Energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement. For a constant force, work depends on the component of force parallel to motion. | AP questions often test whether a force does **positive**, **negative**, or **zero** work based on angle and displacement. |
| **Net Work** | The total work done by all forces on an object. | This directly connects to the **work-energy theorem**, a core reasoning tool on the exam. |
| **Kinetic Energy** | The energy associated with motion. | You must relate speed changes to energy changes using $$K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$$. |
| **Work-Energy Theorem** | Net work on an object equals the change in kinetic energy. | One of the most important equations in AP Physics 1 for solving motion problems algebraically and conceptually. |
| **Potential Energy** | Stored energy associated with position or configuration, especially **gravitational** and **elastic**. | AP problems frequently require tracking changes in $$U_g$$ and $$U_s$$ across motion. |
| **Conservative Forces** | Forces for which work depends only on initial and final position, not path. | Knowing whether a force is conservative tells you whether **mechanical energy is conserved**. |
| **Conservation of Mechanical Energy** | If only conservative forces do work, then total mechanical energy remains constant. | This is a major shortcut for solving multi-step motion problems without kinematics. |
| **Power** | The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. | AP questions use both average and instantaneous power, including cases with force and velocity. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify the system] --> B[Identify forces doing work]
    B --> C{Are nonconservative forces doing work?}
    C -->|No| D[Use conservation of mechanical energy]
    D --> E["Set $$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$$"]
    E --> F[Solve for speed, height, compression, or position]
    C -->|Yes| G[Include external or nonconservative work]
    G --> H["Use $$W_{nc} = \Delta K + \Delta U$$"]
    H --> I[Solve for the unknown quantity]
    F --> J[If needed, calculate power]
    I --> J[If needed, calculate power]
    J --> K["Use $$P=\frac{W}{\Delta t}$$ or $$P=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Idea** | **Equation / Rule** | **Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Work by a constant force** | $$W = Fd\cos\theta$$ | Use the angle between **force** and **displacement**. |
| **Net work** | $$W_{\text{net}} = \sum W$$ | Add work from all relevant forces. |
| **Kinetic energy** | $$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ | Depends on mass and speed squared. |
| **Work-energy theorem** | $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i$$ | Connects forces and motion through energy. |
| **Gravitational potential energy near Earth** | $$U_g = mgh$$ | Valid when height changes near Earth’s surface. |
| **Elastic potential energy** | $$U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$$ | For springs displaced from equilibrium. |
| **Mechanical energy** | $$E_{\text{mech}} = K + U$$ | Total of kinetic and potential energy. |
| **Conservation of mechanical energy** | $$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$$ | Use when only conservative forces do work. |
| **Energy with nonconservative work** | $$W_{nc} = \Delta E_{\text{mech}} = \Delta K + \Delta U$$ | Useful with friction, applied forces, or drag. |
| **Average power** | $$P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{W}{\Delta t}$$ | Rate of work over a time interval. |
| **Instantaneous power** | $$P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = Fv\cos\theta$$ | Power delivered by a force at an instant. |

### Rules to remember
- **Positive work** increases an object’s kinetic energy.
- **Negative work** decreases an object’s kinetic energy.
- A force perpendicular to displacement does **zero work**.
- **Conservative forces** include **gravity** and **spring force**.
- **Friction** is usually **nonconservative**, so mechanical energy is not conserved when friction does significant work.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Similarities** | **Key Difference** | **AP Use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Work vs. Power** | Both involve energy transfer by forces. | **Work** is total energy transferred; **power** is how fast it is transferred. | Students often compute the correct work but forget to divide by time for power. |
| **Conservative vs. Nonconservative Forces** | Both can change an object’s motion and energy. | Conservative-force work depends only on endpoints; nonconservative-force work depends on path or dissipates mechanical energy. | Determines whether you can use simple mechanical energy conservation. |
| **Kinetic Energy vs. Potential Energy** | Both are forms of energy in mechanics. | **Kinetic** depends on motion; **potential** depends on position or configuration. | AP free-response often asks students to describe energy transformations between these forms. |
| **Work-Energy Theorem vs. Conservation of Mechanical Energy** | Both connect energy to motion. | The **work-energy theorem** is always valid; **mechanical energy conservation** is a special case. | A common AP skill is deciding which method is valid in a given scenario. |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **net work** with the work done by a **single force**. The theorem uses $$W_{\text{net}}$$, not just one contribution.
- Using $$mgh$$ without defining a **reference height** consistently. Only **changes** in gravitational potential energy matter.
- Assuming mechanical energy is always conserved. If **friction**, **drag**, or an external push does work, you must include **nonconservative work**.
- Forgetting that the angle in $$W = Fd\cos\theta$$ is the angle between the **force vector** and **displacement vector**, not the angle of a ramp by itself.
- Treating **power** as the same as **force** or **work**. A large force does not always mean large power; velocity matters in $$P=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can calculate **work** done by a constant force using $$W = Fd\cos\theta$$.
- [ ] I can determine whether a force does **positive**, **negative**, or **zero** work.
- [ ] I can apply the **work-energy theorem** $$W_{\text{net}}=\Delta K$$ to solve for speed or displacement.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **conservative** and **nonconservative** forces.
- [ ] I can use $$U_g=mgh$$ and $$U_s=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$$ appropriately.
- [ ] I can decide when **mechanical energy is conserved** and write $$K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f$$.
- [ ] I can include **nonconservative work** using $$W_{nc}=\Delta K+\Delta U$$ when friction or applied forces are present.
- [ ] I can calculate **average** and **instantaneous power** using $$P=\frac{W}{\Delta t}$$ and $$P=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$.

options: It is the same for both paths because it depends only on the change in height.

# Unit 4: Linear Momentum

## Overview
This unit focuses on **linear momentum**, how forces acting over time change motion through **impulse**, and how momentum is used to analyze **collisions** and other interactions between objects. It matters on the AP Physics 1 exam because these ideas connect **Newton’s laws**, **conservation principles**, and **multi-object systems**, especially in free-response and ranking/comparison questions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear momentum** | A vector quantity defined as mass times velocity: $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ | You must track both **magnitude** and **direction** when analyzing interacting objects and systems. |
| **Impulse** | The effect of a force acting over a time interval: $$\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{p} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$$ | AP questions often ask how changing **force** or **time of contact** affects motion or safety outcomes. |
| **Impulse-momentum theorem** | The net impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}}\Delta t = \Delta \vec{p}$$ for constant net force | This is the main bridge between **forces** and **momentum changes**. |
| **System momentum** | The total momentum of all objects in a chosen system: $$\vec{p}_{\text{sys}} = \sum \vec{p}_i$$ | Choosing the right **system** is essential for determining whether momentum is conserved. |
| **Conservation of momentum** | If net external impulse on a system is zero, total momentum remains constant | This is the core tool for solving **explosions**, **recoils**, and **collisions**. |
| **Elastic collision** | A collision in which both **momentum** and **kinetic energy** are conserved | AP may ask you to distinguish elastic from inelastic interactions conceptually and mathematically. |
| **Inelastic collision** | A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not | Very common on the exam; students must know that **momentum** can be conserved even when **kinetic energy** decreases. |
| **Perfectly inelastic collision** | A special inelastic collision where objects stick together after impact | Frequently tested because it leads to a shared final velocity and clear momentum equations. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose the system] --> B[Identify external forces during the interaction]
    B --> C{"Is external impulse negligible?"}
    C -->|Yes| D[Conserve total momentum of the system]
    C -->|No| E[Use impulse-momentum theorem for object or system]
    D --> F[Relate before-collision and after-collision velocities]
    F --> G{"Type of collision?"}
    G -->|Elastic| H[Momentum conserved and kinetic energy conserved]
    G -->|Inelastic| I[Momentum conserved but kinetic energy changes]
    G -->|Perfectly inelastic| J[Objects move together with common final velocity]
    E --> K[Compute change in momentum from net force and time]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Rule** | **Expression / Meaning** |
|---|---|
| **Linear momentum** | $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ |
| **Change in momentum** | $$\Delta \vec{p} = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i$$ |
| **Impulse** | $$\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{p}$$ |
| **Impulse from force-time graph** | $$\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$$, which is the **area under the force vs. time graph** |
| **Constant-force impulse** | $$\vec{J} = \vec{F}_{\text{net}}\Delta t$$ |
| **Impulse-momentum theorem** | $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}}\Delta t = \Delta \vec{p}$$ for constant net force |
| **System momentum** | $$\vec{p}_{\text{sys}} = \sum \vec{p}_i$$ |
| **Conservation of momentum** | If $$\vec{J}_{\text{ext}} = 0$$, then $$\vec{p}_{\text{sys},i} = \vec{p}_{\text{sys},f}$$ |
| **Two-object momentum conservation** | $$m_1\vec{v}_{1,i} + m_2\vec{v}_{2,i} = m_1\vec{v}_{1,f} + m_2\vec{v}_{2,f}$$ |
| **Perfectly inelastic collision** | $$m_1\vec{v}_{1,i} + m_2\vec{v}_{2,i} = (m_1 + m_2)\vec{v}_f$$ |
| **Kinetic energy** | $$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ |
| **Elastic collision condition** | $$K_i = K_f$$ in addition to momentum conservation |
| **Newton’s third law connection** | During an interaction, forces are equal and opposite, so internal impulses within the system are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction |

**Key rule:** Momentum conservation applies to a **system**, not automatically to each object individually.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Comparison** | **Momentum** | **Kinetic Energy** | **Key AP Point** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Always conserved?** | Conserved only when net external impulse is zero | Not always conserved | Students often wrongly assume both are always conserved in collisions. |
| **Elastic collision** | Conserved | Conserved | Both equations may be used. |
| **Inelastic collision** | Conserved | Decreases for the system | Some kinetic energy becomes other forms, such as thermal or sound. |
| **Perfectly inelastic collision** | Conserved | Decreases | Objects stick together; use a common final velocity. |

| **Concept Pair** | **How They Are Connected** |
|---|---|
| **Force and impulse** | A larger force or longer interaction time produces a larger impulse: $$\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t$$ for constant force. |
| **Impulse and momentum change** | Impulse is not an extra quantity; it is exactly the object’s **change in momentum**. |
| **System choice and conservation** | Whether momentum is conserved depends on the **system boundary** and whether external impulses are negligible. |
| **Newton’s third law and momentum conservation** | Internal interaction forces come in equal-and-opposite pairs, so internal impulses cancel within the system. |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **momentum conservation** with **kinetic energy conservation**. In many collisions, momentum is conserved while kinetic energy is not.
- Forgetting that **momentum is a vector**. A negative velocity means negative momentum in a chosen coordinate direction.
- Applying conservation of momentum to a situation with a significant **external impulse** without checking the system first.
- Mixing up **force** and **impulse**. A small force over a long time can produce the same impulse as a large force over a short time.
- Assuming that if two objects exert equal and opposite forces, they undergo equal changes in velocity. Their **impulses** are equal in magnitude, but different masses can produce different velocity changes.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define **linear momentum** and calculate it using $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$.
- [ ] Use the **impulse-momentum theorem** to relate force, time, and change in momentum.
- [ ] Interpret the **area under a force-time graph** as impulse.
- [ ] Decide when **momentum is conserved** by checking for negligible **external impulse**.
- [ ] Write and solve a **momentum conservation equation** for a two-object interaction.
- [ ] Distinguish between **elastic**, **inelastic**, and **perfectly inelastic** collisions.
- [ ] Explain why **kinetic energy** is not always conserved even when **momentum** is.
- [ ] Track **direction signs** correctly when solving one-dimensional collision problems.

# Unit 5: Torque and Rotational Dynamics

## Overview
This unit introduces how forces cause **rotation**, not just linear motion. You will study **torque**, **rotational inertia**, **Newton’s second law for rotation**, and the conditions for **static equilibrium**—all of which are common on the AP Physics 1 exam in both conceptual and quantitative questions.

Understanding this unit helps you connect familiar ideas like **force**, **mass**, and **acceleration** to rotating systems such as rods, pulleys, doors, and balanced objects.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Torque** | The rotational effect of a force about a chosen axis or pivot. | AP questions often ask whether a force causes clockwise or counterclockwise rotation and how torque depends on angle and lever arm. |
| **Lever Arm** | The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force. | Students must distinguish between the full distance and the **perpendicular** distance when calculating torque. |
| **Rotational Inertia** | A measure of how difficult it is to change an object’s rotational motion. Depends on mass distribution relative to the axis. | The AP exam emphasizes that mass farther from the axis gives larger rotational inertia, even if total mass is unchanged. |
| **Angular Acceleration** | The rotational analogue of linear acceleration. | Used with torque and rotational inertia in rotational dynamics problems. |
| **Newton’s Second Law for Rotation** | Net torque causes angular acceleration. | A central equation in this unit; often paired with translational motion in pulley or rolling-style setups. |
| **Static Equilibrium** | A rigid body is in equilibrium when both net force and net torque are zero. | Very common in AP free-response and multiple-choice questions involving beams, signs, ladders, and balances. |
| **Center of Mass** | The point where an object’s mass can be treated as concentrated for translational analysis. | Weight often acts at the center of mass, which is crucial for torque calculations and equilibrium setups. |
| **Rotational vs. Translational Quantities** | Parallel ideas connect force to torque, mass to rotational inertia, and acceleration to angular acceleration. | AP Physics 1 often tests whether students can correctly map linear ideas onto rotational ones. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose the system and axis of rotation] --> B[Draw all forces on the rigid body]
    B --> C[Identify each torque direction]
    C --> D["Compute each torque using $$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$ or lever arm"]
    D --> E[Add torques with sign convention]
    E --> F["If rotating: apply $$\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha$$"]
    E --> G["If in equilibrium: set $$\tau_{\text{net}} = 0$$"]
    B --> H["Also check translational motion with $$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$"]
    G --> I["For static equilibrium, also require $$F_{\text{net}} = 0$$"]
    F --> J[Solve for angular acceleration or unknown force]
    I --> K[Solve for unknown support forces, masses, or positions]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Quantity** | **Expression** | **What to Remember** |
|---|---|---|
| **Torque magnitude** | $$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$ | $$r$$ is the distance from axis to point of applied force; $$\theta$$ is the angle between $$\vec{r}$$ and $$\vec{F}$$. |
| **Torque with lever arm** | $$\tau = r_{\perp}F$$ | Use the **perpendicular lever arm** $$r_{\perp}$$. |
| **Rotational Newton’s second law** | $$\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha$$ | Rotational analogue of $$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$. |
| **Static equilibrium: forces** | $$\sum F_x = 0,\quad \sum F_y = 0$$ | No translational acceleration. |
| **Static equilibrium: torques** | $$\sum \tau = 0$$ | No angular acceleration. |
| **Rotational inertia of a point mass** | $$I = mr^2$$ | Mass farther from axis contributes more strongly. |
| **Total rotational inertia** | $$I = \sum mr^2$$ | For several particles or discrete masses. |
| **Tangential acceleration** | $$a_t = \alpha r$$ | Connects rotational and linear motion at radius $$r$$. |
| **Weight force** | $$F_g = mg$$ | Usually acts at the **center of mass** for uniform objects. |

### Sign convention reminder
- Choose **clockwise** or **counterclockwise** as positive and stay consistent.
- A force can be large but still produce **zero torque** if its line of action passes through the pivot.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Linear Motion** | **Rotational Motion** | **Key Connection** |
|---|---|---|
| **Force** $$F$$ | **Torque** $$\tau$$ | Both cause changes in motion. |
| **Mass** $$m$$ | **Rotational inertia** $$I$$ | Both measure resistance to acceleration. |
| **Acceleration** $$a$$ | **Angular acceleration** $$\alpha$$ | Both describe how motion changes with time. |
| $$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$ | $$\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha$$ | These are parallel forms of Newton’s second law. |

### Equilibrium vs. Rotation Caused by a Net Torque

| **Situation** | **Force Condition** | **Torque Condition** | **Result** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Static equilibrium** | $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$ | $$\sum \tau = 0$$ | No linear or angular acceleration |
| **Pure translation only** | $$\sum \vec{F} \neq 0$$ | $$\sum \tau = 0$$ | Object accelerates linearly without angular acceleration |
| **Rotation occurs** | May be zero or nonzero | $$\sum \tau \neq 0$$ | Angular acceleration occurs |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **distance from pivot** with **lever arm**. The correct torque distance is the **perpendicular** distance to the force’s line of action.
- Forgetting that **equilibrium requires both** $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$ **and** $$\sum \tau = 0$$. Zero torque alone is not enough.
- Assuming larger force always means larger torque. A smaller force applied farther from the pivot can produce a greater torque.
- Ignoring the **angle** in $$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$. Maximum torque occurs when the force is perpendicular to the radius.
- Treating **rotational inertia** like ordinary mass only. Two objects with the same mass can have different $$I$$ if their mass is distributed differently.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can define **torque** and determine its direction as clockwise or counterclockwise.
- [ ] I can calculate torque using $$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$ or $$\tau = r_{\perp}F$$.
- [ ] I can explain why the **location of mass** affects **rotational inertia**.
- [ ] I can apply $$\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha$$ to solve for angular acceleration or unknown torque.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **linear** and **rotational** analogies such as $$F$$ vs. $$\tau$$ and $$m$$ vs. $$I$$.
- [ ] I can identify where **weight acts** and use the **center of mass** in torque problems.
- [ ] I can solve **static equilibrium** problems by using $$\sum F_x = 0$$, $$\sum F_y = 0$$, and $$\sum \tau = 0$$.
- [ ] I can avoid common sign and pivot-choice errors when summing torques.

# Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

## Overview
This unit extends linear energy and momentum ideas to **rotational motion**, focusing on **rotational kinetic energy**, **angular momentum**, and the **conservation laws** that govern spinning systems. On the AP Physics 1 exam, these topics often appear in multi-concept problems that connect **torque**, **moment of inertia**, **work**, **energy**, and **collisions involving rotation**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rotational kinetic energy** | Energy associated with an object’s rotation, depending on **moment of inertia** and **angular speed** | Frequently paired with conservation of energy in rolling, spinning, and pulley-style systems |
| **Moment of inertia** | Rotational analogue of mass; measures how mass distribution affects resistance to angular acceleration | AP questions often test how changing mass placement changes rotational motion and energy |
| **Angular momentum** | Rotational analogue of linear momentum; depends on **moment of inertia** and **angular velocity** | Central to collisions, spinning systems, and conservation problems when external torque is negligible |
| **Conservation of angular momentum** | Total angular momentum stays constant if net external torque is zero | Common in skater, turntable, disk, and stick/clay collision scenarios |
| **Work done by torque** | Rotational work transfers energy into or out of rotational motion | Connects torque to changes in rotational kinetic energy |
| **Rolling without slipping** | Motion in which translational and rotational motion are linked | A major AP theme because it combines linear and rotational energy relationships |
| **Translational vs. rotational energy** | A rolling object can have both center-of-mass kinetic energy and rotational kinetic energy | AP problems often ask students to identify where energy is stored in a moving object |
| **External torque vs. internal forces** | Only external torque changes total angular momentum of a system | Important for deciding whether angular momentum is conserved in a given situation |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Identify the system"] --> B["Check for net external torque"]
    B -->|"Net external torque = 0"| C["Use conservation of angular momentum"]
    B -->|"Net external torque not zero"| D["Use torque-angular acceleration relationships"]
    C --> E["Relate initial and final rotation states"]
    D --> F["Find angular acceleration or work by torque"]
    E --> G["Check whether energy is conserved"]
    F --> G
    G -->|"No nonconservative losses"| H["Use mechanical energy conservation"]
    G -->|"Thermal or other losses present"| I["Use energy accounting with losses"]
    H --> J["Connect rotational and translational motion if rolling"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["Solve for speed, angular speed, or final state"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Relationship** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$ | **Rotational kinetic energy** |
| $$L = I\omega$$ | **Angular momentum** for a rigid object rotating about a fixed axis |
| $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$ | Rotational form of Newton’s second law |
| $$W = \tau \Delta \theta$$ | Work done by a constant torque |
| $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K_{\text{rot}}$$ | Rotational work-energy theorem |
| $$L_i = L_f$$ | **Angular momentum is conserved** when net external torque is zero |
| $$K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$ | Total kinetic energy of a rolling rigid body |
| $$v = r\omega$$ | **Rolling without slipping** condition |
| $$a = r\alpha$$ | Linear and angular acceleration relation for rolling without slipping |
| $$I = \sum mr^2$$ | General idea of **moment of inertia**: mass farther from axis contributes more |
| $$U_g = mgh$$ | Gravitational potential energy, often converted into translational and rotational kinetic energy |

### Common moment of inertia forms to know qualitatively
- **Point mass** at distance $$r$$:
  $$I = mr^2$$
- **Hoop / thin ring** about center:
  $$I = MR^2$$
- **Solid disk / solid cylinder** about center:
  $$I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$$
- **Solid sphere** about center:
  $$I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$$

### Big AP rule
If **net external torque is zero**, then angular momentum is conserved even if **kinetic energy is not** conserved.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference / AP Focus** |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear momentum** vs. **Angular momentum** | Both are conserved under the right external conditions | Linear momentum depends on $$mv$$, while angular momentum depends on rotational state and axis choice |
| **Mass** vs. **Moment of inertia** | Each resists acceleration in its respective motion type | Moment of inertia depends not just on total mass but on how far mass is from the axis |
| **Translational kinetic energy** vs. **Rotational kinetic energy** | Both can exist at the same time in rolling motion | AP often asks students to account for both, not just one |
| **Energy conservation** vs. **Angular momentum conservation** | Both are powerful problem-solving tools | One may be conserved while the other is not; students must check conditions separately |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Object moves and rotates"] --> B["Translational KE: $$\frac{1}{2}Mv^2$$"]
    A --> C["Rotational KE: $$\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$"]
    C --> D["Depends on mass distribution"]
    A --> E["Angular momentum: $$I\omega$$"]
    E --> F["Conserved if net external torque is zero"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **energy conservation** with **angular momentum conservation**. A collision may conserve angular momentum but not kinetic energy.
- Forgetting that **moment of inertia** depends on **mass distribution**, not just total mass. An object with more mass farther from the axis is harder to spin up.
- Using $$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ alone for a **rolling object**. Rolling objects usually have both translational and rotational kinetic energy.
- Assuming angular momentum is always conserved. It is conserved only when the **net external torque** on the system is zero.
- Mixing up the rolling condition $$v = r\omega$$ with a universal rule. It applies only for **rolling without slipping**.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can define **rotational kinetic energy** and calculate it using $$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$.
- [ ] I can explain what **moment of inertia** means and how mass distribution affects it.
- [ ] I can determine when **angular momentum is conserved** by checking for **net external torque**.
- [ ] I can use $$L = I\omega$$ to compare initial and final rotational states.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **conservation of energy** and **conservation of angular momentum**.
- [ ] I can analyze **rolling without slipping** using $$v = r\omega$$ and total kinetic energy.
- [ ] I can identify when a system has both **translational** and **rotational** kinetic energy.
- [ ] I can solve AP-style problems involving spinning objects, collisions, or changing rotation rates using the correct conservation law.

For a rigid body about a fixed axis, the net turning effect equals the product of rotational inertia and angular acceleration: $$\tau_{net} = I\alpha$$.

# Unit 7: Oscillations

## Overview
This unit focuses on **oscillatory motion**, especially **simple harmonic motion (SHM)** in **mass-spring systems** and **pendulums**. You’ll study how **restoring forces**, **period**, **frequency**, and **energy transfer** determine the motion of systems that move back and forth about **equilibrium**.

On the AP Physics 1 exam, this unit matters because it connects **forces**, **energy**, and **motion graphs**, and often requires you to reason qualitatively about how changing system variables affects **period**, **amplitude**, and **energy**.

---

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Oscillation** | Repeated motion about an **equilibrium position**. | AP questions often ask you to identify when a system will oscillate and what conditions are required. |
| **Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)** | A special type of oscillation where the **restoring force** is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction. | You must recognize SHM from force or acceleration relationships such as $$F=-kx$$. |
| **Restoring Force** | A force that pulls or pushes an object back toward equilibrium. | AP free-response often asks why motion is oscillatory: the answer depends on the restoring force. |
| **Period and Frequency** | **Period** $$T$$ is time for one cycle; **frequency** $$f$$ is cycles per second. | These are central measurable quantities and often appear in graph interpretation and proportional reasoning. |
| **Mass-Spring System** | An oscillating system where a spring provides the restoring force. | You need to know how $$T$$ depends on **mass** and **spring constant**, not amplitude. |
| **Pendulum Motion** | Oscillation of a bob suspended by a string, approximately SHM for small angles. | AP commonly tests the small-angle condition and how $$T$$ depends on **length** and **gravitational field**. |
| **Energy in SHM** | Energy continuously shifts between **kinetic energy** and **potential energy** while total mechanical energy remains constant in an ideal system. | Many questions ask where energy is greatest or least at different positions in the motion. |
| **Graphs of SHM** | Position, velocity, and acceleration vary periodically and are related by phase shifts. | Students must interpret motion graphs without relying on memorized shapes alone. |

---

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Object displaced from equilibrium"] --> B["Restoring force acts toward equilibrium"]
    B --> C["Object accelerates toward equilibrium"]
    C --> D["Speed increases; kinetic energy increases"]
    D --> E["Passes equilibrium with maximum speed"]
    E --> F["Inertia carries object beyond equilibrium"]
    F --> G["Restoring force reverses direction"]
    G --> H["Object slows; potential energy increases"]
    H --> I["Momentarily stops at maximum displacement"]
    I --> A
```

This cycle describes ideal **oscillatory motion**. The key AP idea is that the object continues past equilibrium not because the restoring force pushes it away, but because of its **inertia**.

---

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Relationship** | **Formula** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Hooke’s Law** | $$F_s=-kx$$ | Spring restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction. |
| **Condition for SHM** | $$F \propto -x$$ | If the net force is linear and directed toward equilibrium, the motion is SHM. |
| **Frequency and Period** | $$f=\frac{1}{T}$$ | Converts between cycles per second and time per cycle. |
| **Angular Frequency** | $$\omega=2\pi f=\frac{2\pi}{T}$$ | Useful for connecting oscillation timing relationships. |
| **Period of Mass-Spring System** | $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$ | Period increases with larger **mass** and decreases with stiffer springs. |
| **Period of Simple Pendulum** | $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$ | Valid for **small-angle oscillations**; period depends on string length and gravity, not mass. |
| **Spring Potential Energy** | $$U_s=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$$ | Maximum at maximum displacement. |
| **Kinetic Energy** | $$K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ | Maximum at equilibrium in ideal SHM. |
| **Total Mechanical Energy in Spring SHM** | $$E=K+U_s=\frac{1}{2}kA^2$$ | Constant in an ideal system; depends on amplitude $$A$$. |
| **Maximum Speed in Spring SHM** | $$v_{\max}=\omega A$$ | Occurs at equilibrium. |
| **Maximum Acceleration in Spring SHM** | $$a_{\max}=\omega^2 A$$ | Occurs at maximum displacement. |

### Must-know rules
- In ideal SHM, **equilibrium** is where **net force** and **acceleration** are zero.
- At **maximum displacement** $$x=\pm A$$, speed is zero and the magnitude of restoring force is greatest.
- At **equilibrium** $$x=0$$, speed is greatest and spring potential energy is least.
- For a **pendulum**, the SHM model is accurate only for **small angles**.

---

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Feature** | **Mass-Spring System** | **Simple Pendulum** | **AP Comparison** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Restoring interaction** | Spring force | Component of gravitational force | Both involve a force that points toward equilibrium. |
| **Period formula** | $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$ | $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$ | Know which variables matter in each system. |
| **Depends on mass?** | Yes, through $$m$$ | No | A classic AP conceptual question. |
| **Depends on amplitude?** | No, for ideal SHM | Approximately no, for small angles | Students often incorrectly include amplitude. |
| **Energy storage** | In **spring potential energy** and **kinetic energy** | In **gravitational potential energy** and **kinetic energy** | Be able to describe energy transformations qualitatively. |
| **SHM always exact?** | Yes, if Hooke’s law holds | Only approximately for small angles | AP may test limits of the model. |

---

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **equilibrium position** with a point where motion stops. In SHM, the object moves **fastest** at equilibrium.
- Assuming the **period** depends on **amplitude**. For ideal springs and small-angle pendulums, it does not.
- Using the **pendulum period formula** for large angles without noting that it is only valid for **small oscillations**.
- Forgetting that the negative sign in $$F=-kx$$ shows **direction**, not that the force is “negative” in magnitude.
- Mixing up where **kinetic energy** and **potential energy** are maximum: $$K$$ is maximum at equilibrium, while potential energy is maximum at the turning points.

---

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can define **oscillation**, **equilibrium**, and **simple harmonic motion**.
- [ ] I can explain why a **restoring force** causes repeated motion about equilibrium.
- [ ] I can use $$f=\frac{1}{T}$$ to relate **frequency** and **period**.
- [ ] I can apply $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$ to a **mass-spring system** and predict how changing $$m$$ or $$k$$ changes the period.
- [ ] I can apply $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$ to a **simple pendulum** and explain the small-angle condition.
- [ ] I can identify where **speed**, **acceleration**, **restoring force**, and **energy** are greatest or least during SHM.
- [ ] I can describe how **kinetic energy** and **potential energy** trade off while total mechanical energy remains constant.
- [ ] I can compare **mass-spring motion** and **pendulum motion** on the basis of force, period, and energy.

# Unit 8: Fluids

## Overview
This unit introduces how **fluids** behave when at rest and in motion, focusing on **density**, **pressure**, **buoyant force**, **continuity**, and **Bernoulli’s equation**. On the AP Physics 1 exam, these ideas are often tested through conceptual reasoning, proportional relationships, and qualitative interpretations of equations rather than heavy computation.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Density** | Mass per unit volume of a substance. | Used to compare materials, predict floating or sinking, and connect mass, volume, and buoyancy. |
| **Pressure** | Force per unit area exerted by a fluid or object. | Central to hydrostatics; students must reason about how pressure changes with depth and area. |
| **Hydrostatic Pressure** | Pressure in a fluid due to the weight of fluid above a point. | Explains why pressure increases with depth and why points at the same depth have the same pressure. |
| **Archimedes’ Principle** | The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. | A major AP concept for floating, sinking, and apparent weight problems. |
| **Buoyancy** | Upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object. | Often tested conceptually with free-body diagrams and comparisons between submerged and floating objects. |
| **Continuity** | For steady flow of an incompressible fluid, flow rate is conserved. | Used to relate fluid speed and cross-sectional area in pipes or streamlines. |
| **Bernoulli’s Equation** | Relates pressure, speed, and height in flowing fluid. | Helps explain pressure-speed tradeoffs and fluid behavior in narrowing pipes or changing elevations. |
| **Ideal Fluid Assumptions** | Fluid is incompressible, nonviscous, and in steady flow. | Students must know when continuity and Bernoulli apply and when real-world complications are ignored. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Fluid properties] --> B[Density determines mass-volume relationship]
    B --> C[Fluid at rest]
    C --> D[Pressure acts in all directions]
    D --> E[Pressure increases with depth]
    E --> F[Pressure difference creates net upward force]
    F --> G[Buoyant force]
    G --> H["Compare buoyant force to weight (float, sink, or suspend)"]

    B --> I[Fluid in motion]
    I --> J[Steady incompressible flow]
    J --> K[Continuity: smaller area gives larger speed]
    K --> L[Apply Bernoulli relationship]
    L --> M[Higher speed often corresponds to lower pressure]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Formula / Rule** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$ | **Density**: mass per unit volume. |
| $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$ | **Pressure**: force distributed over area. |
| $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$ | **Pressure at depth** in a fluid at rest, where $$P_0$$ is surface pressure. |
| $$\Delta P = \rho g \Delta h$$ | Pressure difference between two depths in the same fluid. |
| $$F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{disp}} g$$ | **Buoyant force** equals weight of displaced fluid. |
| $$W = mg$$ | **Weight** of an object; compare to buoyant force to determine motion. |
| $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$ | **Continuity equation** for incompressible steady flow. |
| $$P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g y = \text{constant}$$ | **Bernoulli’s equation** along a streamline for an ideal fluid. |

### High-value AP relationships
- If an object **floats**, then $$F_B = mg$$.
- If an object is **fully submerged**:
  - it **sinks** if $$mg > F_B$$
  - it **rises** if $$F_B > mg$$
  - it is **neutrally buoyant** if $$F_B = mg$$
- For the same fluid, deeper points have greater pressure because $$\Delta P = \rho g \Delta h$$.
- In a narrower section of pipe, fluid speed increases, so by Bernoulli, pressure often decreases.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Related Ideas** | **Connection / Difference** | **AP Takeaway** |
|---|---|---|
| **Density vs Pressure** | Density is a property of a material; pressure depends on force/area or fluid depth. | Do not confuse a substance’s density with the pressure it exerts. |
| **Pressure vs Buoyant Force** | Pressure acts at a point or on a surface; buoyant force is the net upward force from pressure differences. | Buoyancy comes from greater pressure at lower parts of an object than at upper parts. |
| **Floating vs Fully Submerged** | Floating objects displace fluid whose weight equals the object’s weight; submerged objects may displace their full volume. | A floating object does **not** necessarily have buoyant force less than weight; in equilibrium they are equal. |
| **Continuity vs Bernoulli** | Continuity connects **area** and **speed**; Bernoulli connects **pressure**, **speed**, and **height**. | Often used together: first find how speed changes, then infer pressure changes. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Smaller cross-sectional area] --> B[Greater fluid speed]
    B --> C[Lower pressure at same height]
    D[Greater depth] --> E[Greater pressure]
    E --> F[Greater pressure on bottom than top]
    F --> G[Net upward buoyant force]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- **Pressure depends on depth, not container shape.** A tall narrow container and a wide container with the same fluid depth produce the same pressure at the bottom if the fluid is the same.
- **Buoyant force is determined by displaced fluid**, not directly by the object’s mass. For submerged objects, it depends on $$\rho_{\text{fluid}}$$ and $$V_{\text{disp}}$$.
- **Floating objects still have balanced forces.** If an object floats at rest, then $$F_B = mg$$ exactly.
- **A faster fluid speed does not always mean lower pressure everywhere** unless Bernoulli’s assumptions apply and the comparison is along a streamline.
- **Area and pressure are not inversely related in hydrostatics.** Pressure at a given depth is the same regardless of the object’s surface area, though total force can differ because $$F = PA$$.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] Define **density** and use $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$ to solve for mass, volume, or density.
- [ ] Explain how **pressure** depends on force, area, and depth in a fluid.
- [ ] Use $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$ or $$\Delta P = \rho g \Delta h$$ to compare pressures at different depths.
- [ ] State and apply **Archimedes’ principle** to determine **buoyant force**.
- [ ] Determine whether an object will **float**, **sink**, or be **neutrally buoyant** by comparing $$F_B$$ and $$mg$$.
- [ ] Explain why buoyant force arises from a **pressure difference** between the bottom and top of an object.
- [ ] Apply the **continuity equation** $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$ to compare fluid speeds in different sections of a pipe.
- [ ] Use **Bernoulli’s equation** qualitatively or quantitatively to relate **pressure**, **speed**, and **height** in ideal fluid flow.
